# VIctory fork (work in progress)

A work-in-progress fork of [VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory), a
compatibility layer that runs an Xbox Series title natively on Windows from
files the user supplies. This fork follows upstream
`main` and adds fixes aimed at one goal: getting the game's world to render
correctly and playably on one particular PC.

**This repository contains no game files, code or assets.** You need your own
copy of the game. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's
developer or publisher.

## Credits

- **[VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory)** by Marvisak and its
  contributors is the base of everything here: the loader, the runtime
  services, the Direct3D 12 back end and the shader recompiler. Licensed
  GPL-3.0-or-later; so is this fork. Upstream's history is kept intact below
  the single commit that carries this fork's changes.
- **[XCL](https://github.com/ivall/xcl)** by ivall and its contributors
  (GPL-2.0-only) was used as a reference for how the same title behaves under
  another layer. Fixes inspired by it were written anew in VIctory's code.
- The guard over every view of a memory page is code by **myokex**
  ([victory-amd](https://github.com/myokex/victory-amd), commit `c6dc4d8`), which
  adapts pull request #115 here by Spexivus, its correction by joroyt and a part of
  VIctory #1122 by tightfall. The read-beside fix for kernel reads into title
  memory is by **Joshua Odom** (commit `10ea38e` of the same fork family). Both
  are carried here unchanged apart from one merge conflict.
- This fork's changes were developed with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code).

## Status of this fork (2026-11-25)

**Not playable yet: about 8 to 10 frames per second in the first rooms and 5 to 8.5 in the
opening cutscene (the console runs 30), and shadowed areas are black.**
Tested on one machine: Windows 11, Intel i7-14700KF, NVIDIA RTX 4070 12 GB,
32 GB RAM. The Series X profile is used throughout.

| Stage | State in this fork |
|-------|--------------------|
| Boot, menus, start screen | works, 30 fps (as upstream) |
| Opening cutscene | plays from start to finish, in order, lit: title cards, credits cards, night and dusk shots |
| Saves | the game autosaves a checkpoint and loads it again |
| First gameplay scene (the prologue) | renders: characters, textures, sky, sunlit exterior; HUD, pause menu and pad input work |
| Light in shadow | missing: the game's ray-traced bounce light and ray-traced lamp and sun shadows do not run yet, so anything the sun does not hit directly is black |
| Frame rate in the world | 8 to 10 fps in the first rooms: 97 to 104 ms a frame at about 3,850 draws, 122 ms in a heavier view (6,774 draws). 5 to 8.5 fps through the opening cutscene, by stretch (runs 271 to 273, with `VICTORY_CARD_WINDOWS_MB`). All measured with the switch set of run 253, which is off by default: `VICTORY_LEVELS_ON_DEMAND=1 VICTORY_ASYNC_SUBMIT=1 VICTORY_QUEUE2=1 VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW=1 VICTORY_TEXTURE_NO_WAIT=1 VICTORY_MERGE_GAP=64 VICTORY_MERGE_RUNS=4096 VICTORY_STAGING_POOL=0 VICTORY_COPY_PLAIN=1 VICTORY_JOIN_PARTS=1 VICTORY_BACK_OWN_VIEW=1 VICTORY_INDIRECT_GATHER=1 VICTORY_CARD_REHASH_RUNS=1`. The plain defaults were last measured at 420 to 450 ms a frame and not since. It started at 3 to 6 seconds a frame |
| Stability | no driver hang or device loss in normal runs (a hang introduced by the wave64 update was found and fixed: its barrier form for 64-lane programs is now off unless `VICTORY_WAVE_WIDE=1`) |

### Newest (2026-11-25, night UTC)

**Small buffers into the card's memory: about 18 ms of card time a frame gone, 5 ms of frame so far.**
Tested on the machine above, first rooms, at like draw counts (runs 274 and 275).
- **Why some compute passes were slow.** A title buffer's host copy under 1 MiB stayed in the PC's
  memory (about 3,700 of 3,800 copies, 30 MB in all), so every load, store and atomic a shader did
  on it crossed the bus. The passes that were slow by the thread were small dispatches on such
  buffers. `VICTORY_CARD_BUFFERS_MIN_KB=64` (with `VICTORY_CARD_BUFFERS_MB=1280`; off by default)
  puts every copy in the card's memory: the title's lists went from 68.0 to 49.8 ms of card time a
  frame; single passes from 6.7 to 1.6 ms, from 4.1, 2.7 and 2.0 ms to under 0.3 each. The frame:
  114.9 -> 109.7 ms. The layer's own send-and-hash lists rose from 11.6 to 23.0 ms (each small copy
  is hashed over a whole 64 KiB); `VICTORY_CARD_HASH_LEN=1` hashes the buffer's own bytes instead
  and has not run in a game yet. The card now idles 12 to 40 ms a frame: the thread that prepares
  submissions is the limit.
- **`changed_runs` by masks** (the default; `VICTORY_CHANGED_RUNS=0` the old walk, `=alt` in turn):
  64 bytes at a time as one mask of differing bytes. 3.8 ms less work a frame on the submitting
  thread at equal draws; the frame's gain is inside the noise. A first form (64 equal bytes, then
  eight at a time) was a fifth slower than the walk on sparse changes and never ran.
- **Scalar buffer loads, four dwords a call** (`VICTORY_SHADER_OPT=127`; not in the default 63):
  the dwords of one console load instruction are read by one call. Whole pack: with the bit off
  25,635 of 25,635 shaders are byte-identical to the build before; with it on 20,154 change and
  buffer loads fall by 38 %. Tested on the software adapter, also across a view's end. Whether a
  card is faster for it is not measured yet.

oss.readme:
# VIctory

Runs Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series X|S) natively on Windows, from files
the user supplies.

The title's x86-64 code runs unchanged inside our process; VIctory supplies
the platform underneath it and converts the title's data, ahead of time where
it can (shaders and pipelines too, see Getting started) and on first use
otherwise. See [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

## Status (2026-11-25)

**Not playable yet, but you can get into the game.** The title boots, runs
its menus at its own 30 fps, loads the world, plays the intro cutscene and
reaches the **prologue**, the mission after it, with the graphics fully
displayed, at about **1 frame per second**.

| Stage | State |
|-------|-------|
| Boot, first-boot screens (accessibility, language, settings, legal) | works, 30 fps |
| Intro video with sound | works |
| Start screen, profile and saves | works |
| Loading into the world (about a minute) | works |
| The intro cutscene | plays at about 1 fps (0.9-1.0 s a frame, warm cache, quiet machine): textured and lit characters with whole hair, buildings, sky, depth of field, the title card, credits and interface. Missing: ray-traced shadows and indirect light, the local-light shadow mask. Seen in some shots: a pink band over nearer bodies, a stand-in head on a secondary character for a few frames |
| The prologue | reached; the graphics are fully displayed, at about 1 fps |

In the intro cutscene at 1 fps the opening credits land over other shots than
on a console: they follow the frame count, the shots follow the clock.

Tested on one machine: Windows 11, AMD RX 6700 XT (12 GB).

> **Warning.** Entering the world on a real GPU hung it in earlier builds,
> and Windows then reset the display driver (every monitor goes black for a
> moment). The latest runs, several minutes each in the world, did not, but
> it is not ruled out; a run can also end on a GPU fault (`crashes.log`). A
> diagnostics build with `VICTORY_D3D12_WARP=1` renders on the software
> adapter instead (too slow to reach the world in minutes).

What each part does today and what it still needs:

| Subsystem | Today | Needs |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| Loader | Runs the title's executable and its DLLs in our process; crash reports name the faulting code and are kept in `crashes.log` | – |
| Runtime services | One signed-in offline user, licences, packages, saves that survive a kill at any step, text entry dialog | Speech is silent; the dialog and relaunch are untested live |
| Network | Offline by design: the title cannot reach the network | – |
| Files and streaming | Archives and streamed data read, zlib and BCPack decoded in parallel | Loading is limited by writes into title memory |
| Input | XInput pads, keyboard, keyboard stand-in pad | Trigger rumble |
| Audio | Menu, video and loading sound; XMA voices and Opus streams decode | Reverb is silent; Opus results unverified against the title |
| GPU: menus | Draws, compute and presentation on host D3D12; only changed title memory is copied | Frame pacing drifts on one screen in release builds |
| GPU: world | The scene is drawn and presented: mesh pipelines, indirect execution, views the shaders pick from the heap themselves, title memory read by address, depth written from compute, lists that wait for values other queues write, textures made when a shader first reads them, pipelines pre-built or made by worker threads and kept on disk | The title's ray-tracing structures are never built (no ray-traced shadows or indirect light in the intro cutscene); about 1 s a frame; draws of untranslated shaders are dropped; real queries, depth bounds, HDR and scaling are missing |
| Shaders | Console GPU code recompiled to DXIL, ahead of time (`translate --cache`) or at first use, cached on disk. Menus: all. World: all but under 300 of 24,387 programs | Merged geometry stages (195 programs) and under 100 others; fused multiply-adds follow the host GPU; some compute programs need a GPU with 64-lane waves |
| Textures | Console tiled layouts and detiling for the modes the title uses | Render-target metadata planes |
| Series S mode | Menus, loading and the world run with the PC upscaler (`VICTORY_FIDELITYFX_DIR`, about 1 s a frame) | The title's own upscaler DLLs: six of their passes are untranslated, so their picture is wrong |

## Getting started

Requirements: Windows 10/11 x64, a CPU with AVX2, a Direct3D 12 GPU with
shader model 6.6 (and mesh shaders for the world), Rust (pinned in
`rust-toolchain.toml`).

To install Rust, use rustup (`winget install --id Rustlang.Rustup -e`, or
the installer from https://rustup.rs). The first `cargo` command in this
repository then fetches the pinned toolchain. Building needs the MSVC C++
build tools: Visual Studio or its Build Tools with the "Desktop development
with C++" workload.

Keep the build paths short. From a checkout about 170 characters deep, the
`blake3` dependency's build script fails in `ml64.exe` with
`A1009: line too long`, even with long paths enabled in Windows, because
its object files land under `target`. Set `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` to a short
absolute path (`$env:CARGO_TARGET_DIR = 'C:\vt'`; `victory.exe` is then
in `C:\vt\release` instead of `target\release`), or check out the
repository nearer the drive's root.

A run in the world takes about 33 GB of Windows commit (RAM plus paging
file) and about 10 GB of video memory. The tested machine has 32 GB of RAM
and a commit limit of about 80 GB. Check **Committed** under **Task Manager →
Performance → Memory**. If `crashes.log` reports Windows error 1455, close
other applications or increase the Windows paging file size, then retry.

```powershell
cargo xtask install-hooks                # asset-policy check on every commit
copy victory.example.toml victory.toml   # then set your paths (outside the repo)
cargo test --workspace                   # needs no game data
cargo run -p victory -- config           # check your paths
```

oss.readme:
# PortWatch VI

**Does GTA VI run on PC yet?** A static GitHub Pages site that tracks every serious community effort to recompile, emulate or port the leaked Xbox Series build of GTA VI to PC. All efforts are scored on one ladder, and a scout refreshes the data every 3 hours.

- One headline progress bar shows the closest effort, with the top projects pinned to it.
- A live countdown runs to the missing executable's expected drop.
- A leaderboard card per effort shows its own bar, milestone ladder, groundwork breakdown, what works and what's blocking.
- Further sections cover the watchlist of early projects, a toolkit of asset tools, the scout's inbox of new candidates, and fake-download warnings.

No game files, keys or executables are hosted or linked, ever.

## Deploy on GitHub Pages

1. Create a new GitHub repository and push this folder to its `main` branch.
2. In the repo, open **Settings → Pages** and set **Source** to **GitHub Actions**.
3. Open **Settings → Actions → General** and make sure workflows are allowed.
4. Open **Actions → Scout → Run workflow** to run the first scout. It commits fresh data and deploys the site.

Each deploy also runs `scripts/build-site.mjs`, which turns `data/tracker.json` into pages search engines can read: one page per news story (`news/.html`), a news archive, an RSS feed (`news/feed.xml`) and `sitemap.xml`. It then pings [IndexNow](https://www.indexnow.org/) (Bing, Yandex and others; no account needed) with the URLs that changed since the last deploy. For Google, add the site in Search Console and submit `sitemap.xml`.

From then on, `Scout` runs every 3 hours (00:17, 03:17, 06:17 … UTC) on GitHub's servers, so no computer of yours needs to be on. Any push to `main` redeploys the site through `Deploy site`. To change the frequency, edit the `cron` line in `.github/workflows/scout.yml`. For example, `17 6 * * *` runs it once a day. GitHub can delay scheduled runs by a few minutes when it's busy.

## What the scout does (`scripts/scout.mjs`)

1. **Refreshes** every tracked repo: stars, forks, issues, last push, commits in the last 7 days, and whether it's gone (404, or 451 for a DMCA block). It also hashes each README to notice changes.
2. **Spots claims.** If a README newly says GTA VI boots, reaches the menu or runs at some FPS, the card shows an "unverified claim" banner and the change feed records it.
3. **Discovers** new repos from GitHub and GitLab searches (`scout.queries` in `data/tracker.json`), Hacker News, Bluesky, Mastodon, Lemmy and 4chan, plus Reddit and X when keys are set, by pulling GitHub links out of posts. It also gathers **headlines** from the Google News and Bing News feeds, keeping only stories about the leak, ports, takedowns, scams or official news. And it **watches GitHub's public DMCA log** for new Take-Two or Rockstar notices, flagging any tracked project they name. On 4chan it uses the free read-only API, at one request per second. oss.readme:
# xnulinux

Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.

xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel
module (`xnu.ko`) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS
processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its
memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (`fki.ko`).

With a stock Ubuntu kernel, `insmod xnu.ko` boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the
desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.

![macOS and Linux userspace side by side](docs/images/macos-and-linux.jpg)

*One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (`sw_vers`, the Darwin kernel, launchd,
WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,
Linux 7.0, the `xnu` and `fki` modules loaded, and the `insmod xnu.ko` process the macOS kernel runs in).
Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.*

![The hosted macOS desktop](docs/images/desktop.jpg)

*The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).*

| | |
|---|---|
| ![Safari on Wikipedia's XNU article](docs/images/safari-xnu.jpg) | ![Safari on kernel.org](docs/images/safari-kernel-org.jpg) |
| ![Safari on GitHub](docs/images/safari-github.jpg) | |

*Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the
hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (`GPU=auto`).*

![Hosted macOS running on bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark](docs/images/dgx-spark.jpg)

*Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux `7.0.0-1025-nvidia`): hosted macOS 27 running with
4 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM (CPU rendering), shown over macOS Screen Sharing alongside an SSH session from the DGX Spark
host into the hosted Darwin userspace.*

![About This Mac and sysctl on bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark](docs/images/dgx-spark-about.jpg)

*Inside the hosted macOS on DGX Spark: About This Mac (`Chip: Unknown`, `7.80 GB` memory, `macOS Golden Gate 27.2`)
alongside `sysctl machdep.cpu` (`ARM processor`, `hw.cpufamily: 0`, `hw.ncpu: 4`) and `hw.optional.arm`.*

## How it works

```
 macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...)    Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...)
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────    ────────────────────────────────────────────
 XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts)  │
   ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)
 xnu.ko   (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)
   ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)
 fki.ko   (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)
 Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)
```

- **CPUs**: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host
  (idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and `fki.ko` forwards the faults and user exceptions of
  XNU code to XNU's handlers.
- **Memory**: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux
  share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).
- **Devices**: kexts in `kexts/` give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a
  keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.
- **GPU**: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on `gpu/xnu-cpu-metal` (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux
  host's GPU through the DRM bridge (`kexts/XnuDrm` → host call → `gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd` → the Linux render node), using
  Mesa's Venus driver; without a supported DRM bridge backend it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.

## Status

Working on two arm64 Linux setups:

- **Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux VM (`krunkit`, 1 to 6 hosted CPUs)**:
  - macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac:
    49 s).
  - Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes,
    Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.
  - Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each
    run's log kept in `/var/log/xnulinux/`.
  - The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (`Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)`) and is enabled by default
    (`GPU=auto`) when a virtio-gpu render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (`GPU=off`) otherwise.
- **Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux `7.0.0-1025-nvidia`)**:
  - Boots to the full macOS desktop (Screen Sharing and SSH working) directly on bare-metal arm64 Linux with `CPUS=4`
    and 8 GiB of RAM reserved for XNU.
  - Currently renders on the CPU (Mesa lavapipe, `GPU=off`): `xnudrmd` only forwards `virtio-gpu` (Venus) ioctls today,
    so hardware GPU pass-through on the GB10 GPU requires a new DRM bridge backend.

Shipping it as a hosted service (what is distributed, what a user installs to run Apple's macOS) is in
[`docs/hosted-service.md`](docs/hosted-service.md).

What is still a stopgap is listed in [`docs/production.md`](docs/production.md). Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into
the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).

## Requirements

  kernel). Tested on:
